title: Abbreviated Syllabus
text:
Understanding statistics is vitally important for work in Psychology. Data analytic techniques form the bedrock for many avenues of scientific research, and understanding their theory implies knowing when a particular approach is appropriate and, more critically, when it is not.
In Introduction to Data Analysis in Psychology, students gain a foundation for conducting research, interpreting results, and understanding more complex statistical models used in psychology.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
Week 6 turns the probability framework from Week 5 into a formal decision-making procedure.
In Week 5, the course asked:

How unusual is a sample mean if it came from a particular population?

Week 6 now asks:

Is the observed sample mean unusual enough that we should doubt the population model we started with?

That is the basic logic of hypothesis testing.
The lecture frames hypothesis testing as a way to use sample data to evaluate claims about population parameters. If a treatment has no effect, sample means should behave as expected under the original population model. If the treatment changes the population, the observed sample mean may fall far enough from the null expectation to be considered unlikely under that model (Sigal, 2026).
The main conceptual sequence is:
Null model
↓
Sampling distribution under the null
↓
Decision criterion (())
↓
Observed sample mean / test statistic
↓
p value and decision
↓
Errors and power
↓
Effect size and confidence intervals
A central principle of Week 6 is:

Statistical significance is only one part of interpretation.

The lecture ends by emphasizing an ensemble of evidence: p values, effect sizes, confidence intervals, context, and graphical displays should be considered together rather than treating a p value as the entire result (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
section: 1. Review: Individual Score vs. Sample Mean
text:
1. Review: Individual Score vs. Sample Mean
Suppose a population has:
\[
\mu=200,\quad \sigma=25.
\]
For an individual score:
\[
X=205,
\]
the z score is:
\[
z
=
\frac{205-200}{25}
=
0.20.
\]
But if:
\[
\bar X=205
\]
for a sample of:
\[
n=100,
\]
then:
\[
SE
=
\frac{25}{\sqrt{100}}
=
2.5,
\]
and:
\[
z
=
\frac{205-200}{2.5}
=
2.00.
\]
The raw difference is the same—5 points—but the sample mean is much more unusual because sample means fluctuate less than individual scores (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
section: 2. The Big Idea of Hypothesis Testing
text:
2. The Big Idea of Hypothesis Testing
The lecture defines hypothesis tests as procedures that use sample data to evaluate hypotheses about population parameters (Sigal, 2026).
The reasoning is:

If the null model is correct, sample means should usually fall near the null population mean.
If the observed sample mean falls far enough away, it becomes difficult to explain as ordinary sampling error.
We then have evidence against the null model.

Hypothesis testing therefore formalizes the question:

How compatible are the observed data with the null model?

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
3. The Null and Alternative Hypotheses
The null hypothesis states that the population parameter remains at the null value.
Example:
\[
H_0:\mu=262.
\]
The lecture describes this as the claim that the treatment did not change the population.
The alternative hypothesis states the competing possibility.
For a nondirectional test:
\[
H_1:\mu\ne262.
\]
For a directional test:
\[
H_1:\mu>262
\]
or:
\[
H_1:\mu<262.
\]
The hypotheses concern population parameters, not merely the observed sample mean (Sigal, 2026; Privitera, 2018, 2024).

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
4. Why Begin With the Null?
The null hypothesis provides the reference distribution.
We assume (H_0) is true long enough to ask:

If this null model were correct, how likely would our sample result be?

The textbooks use a courtroom analogy: the null is treated as the starting assumption, and the burden is on the data to provide sufficient evidence against it (Privitera, 2018, 2024).
This does not mean the null is believed to be literally true.
It means it is the model against which the observed sample is evaluated.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
5. The Steps of Hypothesis Testing
The lecture presents the process as:

Specify the hypotheses.
Specify the decision criteria.
Collect data.
Calculate the appropriate statistical test.
Make a decision and interpret it (Sigal, 2026).

Privitera organizes the core inferential logic into four formal steps:

State the hypotheses.
Set the criteria for a decision.
Compute the test statistic.
Make a decision (Privitera, 2018, 2024).

These are compatible frameworks. The lecture simply makes the data-collection stage explicit.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
section: 6. Hypothesis Testing as a Sampling-Distribution Problem
text:
6. Hypothesis Testing as a Sampling-Distribution Problem
The logic of Week 6 depends on Week 5.
If the null is true, the sampling distribution of the mean is centered at the null value:
\[
\mu_{\bar X}=\mu_0.
\]
Its standard error is:
\[
SE_{\bar X}
=
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Hypothesis testing asks where the observed sample mean falls in this null sampling distribution.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
7. The Alpha Level
The lecture introduces the alpha level:
\[
\alpha.
\]
A common convention is:
\[
\alpha=.05.
\]
Alpha defines outcomes that are sufficiently unlikely under the null model to fall in a rejection region (Sigal, 2026).
For a two-tailed z test at:
\[
\alpha=.05,
\]
the critical values are:
\[
z=\pm1.96.
\]
The middle 95% corresponds to values that are not in the rejection regions.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
8. Critical Values and Rejection Regions
A critical value marks the boundary of a rejection region.
For a two-tailed z test with:
\[
\alpha=.05,
\]
the two rejection regions each contain:
\[
\frac{.05}{2}
=
.025.
\]
So:
\[
z_{\text{crit}}=\pm1.96.
\]
An obtained test statistic beyond one of these values falls in a rejection region.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
section: 9. Translating Critical z Values Back to Raw Units
text:
9. Translating Critical z Values Back to Raw Units
Suppose:
\[
\mu=262,\quad \sigma=20,\quad n=30.
\]
Then:
\[
SE
=
\frac{20}{\sqrt{30}}
\approx3.65.
\]
For a two-tailed test at ():
\[
z_{\text{crit}}=\pm1.96.
\]
Convert these boundaries back to sample-mean units:
\[
\bar X_{\text{upper}}
=
262+1.96(3.65)
\approx269.2,
\]
and:
\[
\bar X_{\text{lower}}
=
262-1.96(3.65)
\approx254.8.
\]
Sample means beyond these cutoffs fall in the critical regions (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
section: 10. Type I and Type II Errors
text:
10. Type I and Type II Errors
Hypothesis testing can produce correct or incorrect decisions.



Truth
Fail to reject (H_0)
Reject (H_0)




(H_0) true
Correct decision
Type I error


(H_0) false
Type II error
Correct decision




Type I error
Rejecting a true null hypothesis.
Its probability is controlled by:
\[
\alpha.
\]


Type II error
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis.
Its probability is:
\[
\beta.
\]
(Privitera, 2018, 2024; Sigal, 2026)

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
11. False Positives and False Negatives
The lecture uses The Boy Who Cried Wolf to make the error types intuitive.

Type I error
Concluding there is an effect when there is not one.
A false positive.


Type II error
Failing to detect an effect that is actually present.
A false negative.
The analogy is memorable, but the statistical definitions should remain primary.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
12. Power
Power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis.
It is:
\[
1-\beta.
\]
Conceptually:

Power is the probability that the study will detect an effect when the effect is genuinely present.

Privitera notes that .80 is a common planning target for power in behavioral research (Privitera, 2024).

Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
14. What Drives Statistical Significance?
The lecture summarizes several influences on a test statistic and significance:

magnitude of the mean difference;
population standard deviation;
sample size;
chosen alpha;
number of tails (Sigal, 2026).

For the one-sample z test:
\[
z
=
\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}
{\sigma/\sqrt n}.
\]
This formula makes the relationships visible.
A larger numerator increases (|z|).
A smaller denominator also increases (|z|).

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
section: 15. Sample Size and the Same Observed Effect
text:
15. Sample Size and the Same Observed Effect
The Week 6 worksheet provides a particularly important example.
Population:
\[
\mu=60,\quad \sigma=10.
\]
Observed sample mean:
\[
\bar X=63.
\]

If (n=25)
\[
SE
=
\frac{10}{5}
=
2.
\]
Then:
\[
z
=
\frac{63-60}{2}
=
1.50.
\]
At (), two-tailed:
\[
|1.50|<1.96.
\]
So we fail to reject (H_0).


If (n=100)
\[
SE
=
\frac{10}{10}
=
1.
\]
Then:
\[
z
=
\frac{63-60}{1}
=
3.00.
\]
Now:
\[
|3.00|>1.96,
\]
so we reject (H_0).
The sample mean and raw difference are unchanged.
Only sample size changes.
The larger sample produces a smaller standard error and greater power. fileciteturn11file0L35-L45

18. The z Test Statistic
For a sample mean:
\[
z
=
\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}
{SE_{\bar X}}
\]
where:
\[
SE_{\bar X}
=
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Therefore:
\[
z
=
\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}
{\sigma/\sqrt n}.
\]
The statistic tells us how many standard errors the observed sample mean lies above or below the null mean.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
19. Worked Reaction-Time Example
The lecture uses:
\[
\mu_0=262,\quad \sigma=20,\quad n=30,
\]
with observed sample mean approximately:
\[
\bar X=274.5.
\]
First:
\[
SE
=
\frac{20}{\sqrt{30}}
\approx3.65.
\]
Then:
\[
z
=
\frac{274.5-262}{3.65}
\approx3.42.
\]
Because:
\[
3.42>1.96,
\]
for a two-tailed test at (), the observed mean falls beyond the upper critical value.
The lecture therefore rejects the null hypothesis and concludes that the treatment affected reaction time (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
20. The p Value
A p value is interpreted under the null model.
Privitera defines it as the probability of obtaining a sample outcome as extreme as the observed outcome, given that the null hypothesis is true (Privitera, 2018, 2024).
The important structure is:

Assume (H_0), then evaluate how unusual the observed result is.

A p value is not the probability that the null hypothesis itself is true.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
21. Decision Language
The preferred decisions are:

reject (H_0);
fail to reject (H_0).

Do not say:

“We proved the null is true.”

Failing to reject means:

The data did not provide sufficient evidence against the null model under the chosen decision rule.

The 2024 Privitera edition explicitly emphasizes this wording and warns that a failure to reject does not prove the null hypothesis (Privitera, 2024).

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
22. One-Tailed and Two-Tailed Tests

Two-tailed test
Used for a nondirectional alternative:
\[
H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0.
\]
At:
\[
\alpha=.05,
\]
the critical values are:
\[
\pm1.96.
\]


One-tailed test
Used for a directional alternative such as:
\[
H_1:\mu>\mu_0
\]
or:
\[
H_1:\mu<\mu_0.
\]
At:
\[
\alpha=.05,
\]
the critical value is approximately:
\[
1.645
\]
or:
\[
-1.645
\]
depending on direction.
(Sigal, 2026; Privitera, 2018, 2024)

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
23. Why Directionality Matters
For a two-tailed test, alpha is divided between both tails.
For a one-tailed test, all alpha is placed in one tail.
That makes the critical threshold less extreme in the predicted direction and can increase power.
But a one-tailed test requires a defensible directional hypothesis established before examining the results.
Privitera also notes the possibility of a Type III error for one-tailed tests when the effect occurs in the opposite direction from the rejection region (Privitera, 2018, 2024).

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
section: 24. Worksheet Logic Check: One-Tailed vs. Two-Tailed
text:

The key points are:

a two-tailed .05 test places .025 in each tail;

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
25. Worked Maze Example
The lecture asks whether a cold medicine changes maze-completion time.
Population:
\[
\mu=200,\quad \sigma=10.
\]
Sample:
\[
n=4,\quad \bar X=195.
\]
Hypotheses:
\[
H_0:\mu=200
\]
\[
H_1:\mu\ne200.
\]
At:
\[
\alpha=.05,
\]
two-tailed:
\[
z_{\text{crit}}=\pm1.96.
\]
Compute:
\[
SE
=
\frac{10}{\sqrt4}
=
5.
\]
Then:
\[
z
=
\frac{195-200}{5}
=
-1.
\]
Because:
\[
-1
\]
is not beyond:
\[
-1.96,
\]
we fail to reject the null hypothesis (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
section: 26. Why Statistical Significance Is Not Enough
text:
26. Why Statistical Significance Is Not Enough
With a large enough sample, even a small effect can become statistically significant.
Therefore significance does not answer:

How large or important is the effect?

The lecture explicitly introduces effect size for this reason (Sigal, 2026).
The 2024 Privitera edition makes the broader point that researchers should report not only whether an effect exists, but also:

its size;
where it is likely to be located;
how likely the study is to detect it (Privitera, 2024).

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
section: 27. Cohen’s (d) for the One-Sample z Test
text:
27. Cohen’s (d) for the One-Sample z Test
For a one-sample z test:
\[
d
=
\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{\sigma}.
\]
Compare this with the z statistic:
\[
z
=
\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}.
\]
The difference is crucial:

(z) uses standard error;
(d) uses the population standard deviation.

As a result, (d) is not mechanically inflated by sample size in the same way the test statistic is.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
28. Reaction-Time Effect Size
For the lecture example:
\[
\bar X=274.5,\quad \mu_0=262,\quad \sigma=20.
\]
Then:
\[
d
=
\frac{274.5-262}{20}
=
0.625.
\]
Interpretation:

The observed mean differs from the null population mean by approximately 0.625 population standard deviations.

The lecture uses common heuristic benchmarks:

around 0.2–0.3 → small;
around 0.5 → medium;
around 0.8 or above → large (Sigal, 2026).

These are rough conventions, not universal definitions of practical importance.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
29. Significance vs. Effect Size
These answer different questions.

Hypothesis test

Is the observed result sufficiently inconsistent with the null model?



Effect size

How large is the observed difference on a standardized substantive scale?

A result can be:

statistically significant but small;
not statistically significant but potentially meaningful in a low-powered study.

This is why results should not be interpreted from p values alone.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
30. Confidence Intervals
The lecture defines a 95% confidence interval using repeated sampling:

If repeated samples were taken and a 95% CI were computed for each sample, approximately 95% of those intervals would contain the population parameter (Sigal, 2026).

This is a property of the procedure.
It is not the claim that, after one interval has been computed, there is a 95% probability that a fixed population parameter moves in or out of that particular interval.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
section: 31. Confidence Interval Formula for the z Setting
text:
31. Confidence Interval Formula for the z Setting
For a population mean with known ():
\[
CI
=
\bar X
\pm
z_{\text{crit}}SE.
\]
For a 95% CI:
\[
z_{\text{crit}}=1.96.
\]
So:
\[
CI_{95}
=
\bar X
\pm
1.96
\left(
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
\right).
\]

text:
32. Reaction-Time Confidence Interval
Using:
\[
\bar X=274.5,
\]
and:
\[
SE\approx3.65,
\]
the lecture calculates:
\[
CI_{95}
=
274.5
\pm
1.96(3.65).
\]

\[

\approx7.15.

Therefore:
\[
CI_{95}

\]

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
33. What Determines CI Width?
The lecture identifies three main influences:

Sample size
As:
\[
n\uparrow,
\]
standard error decreases, so the CI becomes narrower.


Population variability
As:
\[
\sigma\downarrow,
\]
standard error decreases, so the CI becomes narrower.


Confidence level
Greater confidence requires a more extreme critical value, producing a wider interval.
Thus a 99% CI is wider than a 95% CI for the same data.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
section: 34. Relationship Between Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Tests
text:
34. Relationship Between Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Tests
For a two-tailed test at:
\[
\alpha=.05,
\]
the corresponding interval is a 95% CI.
When the null value is outside the corresponding confidence interval, the result is inconsistent with the null at that significance level.
Privitera (2024) explicitly connects the confidence interval and hypothesis-testing decision in this way.

36. The PHANTOMS Checklist
The lecture provides the mnemonic PHANTOMS as a workflow:

Hypotheses
Assumptions

Test statistic

This is a useful checklist for tutorial work because it prevents students from jumping directly to arithmetic before identifying the inferential structure of the problem.

text:
40. Common Misunderstandings

“Fail to reject means the null is true.”
No.
It means the data did not provide sufficient evidence to reject it.


“p = .03 means there is a 3% probability that the null is true.”
No.
The p value is calculated assuming the null model.


“A significant result must be important.”
No.
Statistical significance and practical importance are different.


“A nonsignificant result means there is no effect.”
Not necessarily.
The study may have had low power.


“Increasing n changes Cohen’s d.”
For the simple one-sample formula used here, no. The sample size affects standard error and the z statistic, not the standardized mean difference (d=(X-)/).


“A smaller alpha always makes a test better.”
No.
A smaller alpha reduces Type I error risk but also makes rejection harder and can reduce power.


“A one-tailed test is always preferable because it has more power.”
No.
It is appropriate only when the directional prediction is substantively justified in advance.

title: Week 06 — Hypothesis Testing, Significance, Effect Size, and Power
text:
41. Tutorial Preparation
A TA should be ready to answer:

“Why do we assume the null is true?”
Because the null provides the reference distribution needed to judge how unusual the observed statistic is.


“What exactly does alpha mean?”
It defines the Type I error rate tolerated by the decision rule under the null model.


“What is a critical region?”
A range of test-statistic values considered sufficiently unlikely under (H_0) to trigger rejection.


“What is the difference between alpha and p?”
Alpha is chosen before seeing the data.
The p value is calculated from the observed data under the null model.


“Why does increasing n make significance easier?”
Because:
\[
SE=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\]
As (n) increases, SE decreases, so the same mean difference becomes larger in standard-error units.


“Why report effect size?”
Because significance answers whether the data conflict with the null model, whereas effect size describes how large the observed effect is.

Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
Week 4 builds directly on Week 3.
Last week, you learned how to describe a distribution using:

measures of central tendency;
measures of shape;
measures of variability.

This week asks the next question:

How can we describe where one particular score sits relative to the rest of a distribution?

The lecture introduces standard scores, especially z scores, as a way to combine information about the center and spread of a distribution into a single interpretable number. A z score tells us whether a raw score is above or below its mean and how many standard deviations away from the mean it lies (Sigal, 2026).
The lecture then connects z scores to the normal distribution and the standard normal distribution, where the mean is 0 and the standard deviation is 1. Once scores are standardized, the z table allows us to translate locations in the distribution into proportions and probabilities (Sigal, 2026; Privitera, 2018).
The lecture’s main intellectual sequence is therefore:
Center + spread
↓
Standard score
↓
z score
↓
Standard normal distribution
↓
z table
↓
Probability / percentile interpretation
A crucial point from the lecture is that standardizing scores does not make a skewed distribution normal. Standardization changes the scale, not the shape (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
1. Population Variance and Standard Deviation
The lecture begins with a direct review of Week 3.
For a population:
\[
\sigma^2
=
\frac{\sum (x_i-\mu)^2}{N}
\]
and:
\[
\sigma
=
\sqrt{
\frac{\sum (x_i-\mu)^2}{N}
}.
\]
The lecture uses:
\[
X=\{1,0,6,1\},
\]
with:
\[
\mu=2.
\]
Then:
\[
SS
=
(1-2)^2+(0-2)^2+(6-2)^2+(1-2)^2
=
22.
\]
Thus:
\[
\sigma^2
=
\frac{22}{4}
=
5.5,
\]
and:
\[
\sigma
=
\sqrt{5.5}
\approx
2.35
\]
(Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
2. Sum of Squares
The lecture explicitly names:
\[
\sum (x_i-\mu)^2
\]
and:
\[
\sum (x_i-\bar{x})^2
\]
as the sum of squares (SS).
Because deviations are squared:

SS can never be negative;
SS equals 0 only if every observation is identical.

If all observations are identical, there is no variation, so variance and standard deviation are also 0 (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
3. Sample Variance and Standard Deviation
For a sample:
\[
s^2
=
\frac{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})^2}{n-1}
=
\frac{SS}{df}.
\]
The standard deviation is:
\[
s
=
\sqrt{
\frac{SS}{n-1}
}.
\]
Using the same data:
\[
SS=22,\quad n=4,
\]
so:
\[
s^2
=
\frac{22}{3}
=
7.33,
\]
and:
\[
s
=
\sqrt{7.33}
\approx
2.71
\]
(Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
4. Why (n-1)?
The lecture gives two complementary explanations.

Estimation explanation
Samples do not fully represent populations, especially at the rare and extreme ends. As a result, sample spread tends to underestimate population spread. Dividing by (n-1) instead of (n) makes the variance estimate larger and improves its performance as an estimate of population variance (Sigal, 2026).


Degrees-of-freedom explanation
Degrees of freedom also refers to the number of values that are independent and “free to vary.”
If the mean and all but one score are known, the final score is determined.
Thus:
\[
df=n-1.
\]

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
5. The Problem With Raw Scores
A raw score in isolation is difficult to interpret.
A score such as:
\[
X=53
\]
could be:

low;
average;
high;

depending on the distribution.
To interpret a raw score, we need to know:

the center;
the spread.

The lecture frames this as the core motivation for standard scores (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
6. What Is a Standard Score?
A standard score combines information about:

center;
spread;

into a single number.
More formally, the lecture describes a standard score as a mean deviation standardized by an average measure of variability (Sigal, 2026).
A standard score tells us two things:

Direction
Is the score above or below the mean?
Distance
How many standard-deviation units separate the score from the mean?

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
7. Standard Scores as Relative Position
A standard score re-expresses a raw score in terms of the distribution it belongs to.
This is important because:
\[
X=80
\]
does not have the same meaning in every distribution.
If one class has:
\[
M=70,\quad SD=5,
\]
then:
\[
X=80
\]
is:
\[
z=\frac{80-70}{5}=2.
\]
That is two standard deviations above the mean.
But if another class has:
\[
M=80,\quad SD=10,
\]
then the same raw score corresponds to:
\[
z=0.
\]
The raw score is identical, but the relative standing is not.

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
8. What Is a z Score?
A z score is a specific kind of standard score.
The lecture defines z scores as a parameterization that transforms a distribution to:
\[
\mu=0
\]
and:
\[
\sigma=1.
\]
For a population:
\[
z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}.
\]
For a sample:
\[
z=\frac{X-\bar{x}}{s}.
\]
A z score is therefore a raw deviation divided by a standard deviation (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
9. Interpreting the Sign of z
The sign tells us direction.

Positive
\[
z>0
\]
means the score is above the mean.


Negative
\[
z<0
\]
means the score is below the mean.


Zero
\[
z=0
\]
means the score is exactly at the mean.

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
10. Interpreting the Magnitude of z
The absolute value tells us the distance from the mean.
Examples:
\[
z=+0.5
\]
means half a standard deviation above the mean.
\[
z=-1
\]
means one standard deviation below the mean.
\[
z=+2
\]
means two standard deviations above the mean.
The lecture explicitly emphasizes that a z score places the raw score into standard deviation units (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
11. Quick Example: Exam Score
Suppose:
\[
M=65,\quad SD=10,\quad X=83.
\]
Then:
\[
z
=
\frac{83-65}{10}
=
1.8.
\]
Interpretation:

The score is 1.8 standard deviations above the mean.

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
section: 12. Which z Score Is Closest to the Mean?
text:
12. Which z Score Is Closest to the Mean?
Suppose the options are:

(z=+0.50)
(z=+1.00)
(z=-1.00)
(z=-2.00)
(z=-0.25)

The score closest to the mean is:
\[
z=-0.25.
\]
Why?
Because the mean corresponds to:
\[
z=0,
\]
and (-0.25) has the smallest absolute distance from 0.

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
13. Standard Scores vs. z Scores
The Week 4 worksheet explicitly asks whether standardized scores and z scores are the same.
They are related, but not identical.
A standard score is the broader category.
A z score is one particular standardized scale with:
\[
M=0,\quad SD=1.
\]
Other standardized scales can use different means and standard deviations.
Examples from the lecture include:

IQ-like scale: (M=100, SD=15)
T-score scale: (M=50, SD=10)
SAT-like scale: (M=500, SD=100)

(Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
14. What Is a Normal Distribution?
The lecture describes the normal distribution as a theoretical curve that is often approximated by real data (Sigal, 2026).
It is defined by two parameters:

a mean;
a standard deviation.

The mean determines the center.
The standard deviation determines the width.

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
17. Normal Does Not Mean Exact
The lecture explicitly treats the normal distribution as theoretical.
Real data may approximate the curve rather than match it perfectly.
The 2018 textbook makes the same point: behavioral data rarely fit the mathematical normal distribution exactly; the normal model is useful when the data are approximately normal (Privitera, 2018).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
section: 18. What Is the Standard Normal Distribution?
text:
18. What Is the Standard Normal Distribution?
If every score in a normal distribution is converted to z scores, the result is the standard normal distribution.
It always has:
\[
\mu=0
\]
and:
\[
\sigma=1.
\]
This is also called:

the z distribution;
the standard normal curve.

(Sigal, 2026; Privitera, 2018)

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
section: 20. Area Under the Curve as Probability
text:
20. Area Under the Curve as Probability
The lecture makes the graphical interpretation explicit:

Probability is represented by area under the normal curve (Sigal, 2026).

Thus:

larger area = larger probability;
smaller tail area = rarer score;
total area under the curve = 1.

This links distribution geometry directly to probability.

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
section: 21. What the z Table Tells Us
text:
21. What the z Table Tells Us
The z table provides proportions associated with z scores.
The lecture uses a table with:

Area between Mean and z
Area beyond z

(see Lecture 4, slide 31).
The 2018 text labels these as:

Column B: area between the mean and z;
Column C: area beyond z toward the tail (Privitera, 2018).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
22. Why Only Positive z Values?
The worksheet asks why the standard normal table includes only positive values.
The answer:

Because the standard normal distribution is symmetrical.

The area associated with:
\[
z=+1.2
\]
mirrors the area associated with:
\[
z=-1.2.
\]
Listing both would be redundant (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
23. Can a Proportion Be Negative?
No.
A probability or proportion must satisfy:
\[
0\le p\le1.
\]
The smallest possible proportion is:
\[
0.
\]
The worksheet answer key explicitly reinforces this point (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
25. Basic Procedure
To find the probability associated with a raw score:

Step 1
Convert the raw score to z.


Step 2
Look up the z score in the z table.


Step 3
Use the appropriate area column based on the diagram.
(Sigal, 2026)

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
26. Example: Proportion Below a Score
Suppose:
\[
\mu=40,\quad \sigma=10,\quad X=35.
\]
Then:
\[
z
=
\frac{35-40}{10}
=
-0.5.
\]
The area between the mean and (z=0.50) is approximately:
\[
0.1915.
\]
Therefore the area below:
\[
z=-0.50
\]
is:
\[
0.5000-0.1915
=
0.3085.
\]
So the proportion below (X=35) is:
\[
0.3085.
\]
This is the correct answer to the lecture concept check (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
27. Example: Between Two Scores
Suppose:
\[
M=195,\quad SD=30,
\]
and we want the percentage between:
\[
X=165
\]
and:
\[
X=225.
\]
Convert:
\[
z_{165}
=
\frac{165-195}{30}
=
-1,
\]
and:
\[
z_{225}
=
\frac{225-195}{30}
=
+1.
\]
The area between (z=-1) and (z=+1) is approximately:
\[
0.6826
\]
or about:
\[
68\%.
\]

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
text:
28. Example: Below the Mean
For any normal distribution:
\[
p(X<M)=0.50.

text:
42. Common Errors With z Scores

“A negative z score means a bad score.”
No. It only means the score lies below the mean.


“A larger raw score always means better relative performance.”
No. Relative standing depends on the mean and standard deviation.


“A z score is the only type of standard score.”
No. It is one specific standardized scale.


“Standardizing makes a distribution normal.”
No. It preserves distribution shape.


“The z table only applies to positive raw scores.”
No. It is based on symmetry around (z=0).


“A negative z score implies a negative probability.”
No. Probabilities remain between 0 and 1.


“If z = 0, the raw score must be 0.”
No. (z=0) means the raw score equals the mean.

title: Week 04 — Standard Scores, Normal Distributions, and Probability
section: 43. Questions a TA Should Be Ready to Answer
text:
43. Questions a TA Should Be Ready to Answer

“Why bother converting to z?”
Because raw scores are hard to interpret without context. z expresses a score relative to its distribution.


“Why divide by SD?”
Because the standard deviation defines the distribution’s unit of spread. Dividing by SD expresses distance from the mean in common units.


“Why is the mean of z always 0?”
Because standardization subtracts the original mean from every score.


“Why is the SD of z always 1?”
Because the deviations are divided by the original standard deviation.


“Why can we use only positive values in the table?”
Because the normal distribution is symmetric.


“Why should I draw the curve?”
Because most z-table mistakes come from choosing the wrong area.


“Why does a skewed distribution stay skewed after standardization?”
Because standardization is a linear transformation.

text:
53. Week 4 Takeaway
The central idea of Week 4 is relative position.
A raw score tells us what was observed.
A z score tells us:

Where that observation sits relative to the rest of its distribution.

The core formula is:
\[
z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}.
\]
From there:

the sign tells us direction;
the magnitude tells us distance;
the standard normal distribution gives us a common scale;
the z table converts distance into probability.

Most importantly:

Standardizing a distribution changes its location and scale, but not its shape.

That distinction becomes essential as the course moves into probability, sampling distributions, and inferential statistics.

Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
Week 2 develops the first major set of descriptive-statistical tools for organizing psychological data. The central question is simple:

Once data have been collected, how should we represent them so that their structure can be understood accurately?

The week begins by reviewing summation notation and then turns to types of variables, scales of measurement, frequency distributions, grouped and ungrouped data, and graphical displays. The assigned readings also introduce central tendency—the mean, median, and mode—as another way to summarize a distribution with a single representative value.
The lecture emphasizes that numerical codes do not automatically determine what mathematical operations are meaningful. The appropriate analysis depends on what the variable actually represents (Sigal, 2026). Privitera (2018, 2024) develops the same general principle through scales of measurement, frequency distributions, and central tendency.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
1. Review: Summation Notation
Week 2 begins by reinforcing a mathematical skill introduced in Week 1: sigma notation.
The full notation
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i
\]
means:

Add the values of variable (X), beginning with the value indexed (i=1) and ending with the value indexed (i=n).

The tutorial stresses that the order of the observations matters when the summation limits refer to specific indices. If
\[
X=\{2,6,4,8,1,7\},
\]
then
\[
\sum_{i=3}^{5}X_i = 4+8+1=13.
\]
Reordering the scores before applying the index would change the problem and produce the wrong answer (PSYC 210 Teaching Team, 2026a).

Sigma and order of operations
Summation notation interacts with BEDMAS/PEDMAS. Parentheses are therefore essential.
Compare:
\[
\sum X_i + 2
\]
with
\[
\sum(X_i+2).
\]
The first expression means “sum the (X) values, then add 2.” The second means “add 2 to every included (X) value, then sum.”
Likewise,
\[
\left(\sum X_i\right)^2
\]
is different from
\[
\sum X_i^2.
\]
The lecture again emphasizes using parentheses to eliminate ambiguity (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
2. Three Useful Summation Rules
The Week 2 applied-practice worksheet reinforces three rules.

Rule 1: Sum of combined variables
\[
\sum(X+Y)=\sum X+\sum Y
\]
provided the same indexed observations are included.


Rule 2: A multiplicative constant can be factored out
\[
\sum(cX)=c\sum X.
\]
For example:
\[
\sum_{i=3}^{6}6Y_i
=
6\sum_{i=3}^{6}Y_i.
\]


Rule 3: A constant added inside the summation is repeated
If there are (k) observations being summed,
\[
\sum(X_i+c)=\sum X_i+kc.
\]
This rule is especially easy to misuse. The constant is added once for each observation included in the summation, not once overall.
The worksheet key applies these rules to paired (X) and (Y) data and also practices products such as (XY), squared sums, and combined expressions (PSYC 210 Teaching Team, 2026a).

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
section: 3. Variables and Why Their Type Matters
text:
3. Variables and Why Their Type Matters
A variable can take more than one value. But different variables carry different kinds of information.
The lecture makes a key point:

The way data are analyzed depends on the variables and on what the numerical values actually represent (Sigal, 2026).

A number can function as:

a label;
a rank;
a measurement with equal units;
a measurement with equal units and a meaningful zero.

The number itself does not tell you which of these applies. You must know how the variable was defined and measured.
For example, coding:

Rock = 1
Pop = 2
Country = 3
Other = 4

does not mean Country is three times Rock. The numbers are labels, not quantities.
This is why scale of measurement matters.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
5. Nominal Variables
A nominal variable separates observations into mutually exclusive categories.
The numbers assigned to categories are simply codes.
Examples include:

preferred browser;
music genre;
type of animal;
political affiliation.

If browser is coded as:

Firefox = 1
Safari = 2
Chrome = 3

then 3 is not “more browser” than 1. The code identifies the category and nothing more.

What can we meaningfully do?
We can count how many observations fall into each category.
We can therefore report:

frequencies;
proportions;
percentages;
the mode.

We cannot interpret arithmetic differences or ratios between category codes.


Important point
A nominal variable can be represented numerically without becoming quantitative. Coding is a data-management choice, not a change in the meaning of the variable (Privitera, 2018, 2024; Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
6. Ordinal Variables
An ordinal variable contains ordered categories.
Examples include:

finishing place in a race;
class rank;
military rank;
letter grades;
ordered response categories.

If:

1 = Gold
2 = Silver
3 = Bronze

then Gold is ranked above Bronze, but the numerical difference between 1 and 3 does not tell us how much better Gold is.
Ordinal measurement gives us:

order without known equal distance between ranks.

This is why the median is often a meaningful measure of central tendency for ordinal data (Privitera, 2018, 2024).

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
7. Interval Variables
An interval variable has ordered values with equal intervals between adjacent units.
The standard example in the Week 2 lecture is Celsius temperature.
The difference between:

(2^C) and (3^C)

represents the same amount of temperature change as the difference between:

(-1^C) and (0^C).

However, Celsius temperature does not have a true zero. (0^C) does not mean “no temperature.”
Therefore, ratio statements are not meaningful:

(10^C) is not twice as hot as (5^C).

Interval variables support meaningful statements about differences, but not arbitrary ratio statements (Privitera, 2018, 2024; Sigal, 2026).

9. Categorical, Discrete, Continuous, Qualitative, and Quantitative
The Week 2 lecture broadly contrasts categorical/discrete variables with continuous/quantitative variables (Sigal, 2026).
Privitera (2018, 2024) makes two separate distinctions:

Discrete vs. continuous

Discrete variables consist of separate values or categories.
Continuous variables can in principle take values anywhere along a continuum.

Examples:

number of siblings → discrete;
reaction time → continuous.



Qualitative vs. quantitative

Qualitative variables differ by category or class.
Quantitative variables differ by amount.

These classifications overlap but are not identical.
For example:

This distinction is useful because “discrete” does not automatically mean “qualitative.”

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
section: 10. A Source Tension: Likert-Like and Rating Scales
text:
10. A Source Tension: Likert-Like and Rating Scales
The Week 2 materials contain a genuine disagreement that should not be hidden.

Lecture framing
The lecture treats Likert-like items critically. It questions whether the psychological distance between adjacent response categories is equal and warns against automatically treating such responses as interval measurements (Sigal, 2026).


Privitera framing
Privitera (2024) explicitly describes rating scales as controversial. The text notes that, under strict measurement rules, individual rating-scale responses may be better viewed as ordinal. However, many behavioral researchers pragmatically treat rating-scale values as interval when equal spacing is assumed, especially for statistical analysis (Privitera, 2024).


What should you learn from this?
Do not memorize “Likert = interval” as an unquestionable rule.
Instead ask:

Is this a single ordered response item or a multi-item scale score?
What assumptions are being made about equal distances between response options?
What convention is the instructor using for this course?
Does the planned statistical analysis require stronger measurement assumptions?

For this course, follow the instructor’s stated conventions on assessed work, but understand that the status of rating-scale data is methodologically debated.

12. Ungrouped Frequency Distributions
An ungrouped frequency distribution lists individual values or categories and the frequency of each one.
A basic table has two columns:



(X)
(f)




value/category
number of occurrences



The first consistency check is:
\[
\sum f = n.
\]
If the sample contains 10 observations, the frequencies must sum to 10.
Ungrouped distributions are especially useful when:

the variable is categorical;
there are only a small number of distinct values;
retaining the exact observed values is useful.

Privitera (2018, 2024) specifically contrasts this with grouped distributions: ungrouped data preserve individual scores/categories; grouped data combine scores into intervals.

13. Frequency, Proportion, Percentage, and Cumulative Values
A full frequency table can include several related summaries.

Frequency
Frequency (f) is the number of observations at a value or in an interval.


Proportion / relative frequency
\[
p=\frac{f}{n}.
\]
The proportions should sum to approximately:
\[
\sum p=1.00.
\]


Percentage
\[
\%=p\times100.
\]
Percentages should sum to approximately:
\[
100\%.
\]


Cumulative frequency
Cumulative frequency is the running total of frequencies.
For an ascending table, it answers:

How many observations scored this value or less?

The final cumulative frequency should equal (n).


Cumulative relative frequency / cumulative percentage
A cumulative relative frequency is the running total of proportions.
A cumulative percentage is the running total of percentages.
The final values should be approximately:
\[
1.00
\]
and
\[
100\%.
\]
respectively (Privitera, 2018, 2024; Sigal, 2026).

2+2+0+3=7=n,
\]
and the final cumulative values are:

CF = 7;
cumulative proportion = 1.00;
cumulative percentage = 100%.

This example shows why a score with frequency zero may still appear in the table: retaining the full sequence makes the structure of the scale clear (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
15. Percentile Rank
Cumulative percentages can be interpreted as percentile ranks.
A percentile rank tells us what percentage of scores fall at or below a specified score under the convention used in the Week 2 materials.
For example, the lecture uses a table of dreams recalled by 50 children. At (X=2), the cumulative frequency is 30:
\[
\frac{30}{50}\times100=60\%.
\]
Thus a score of 2 corresponds to the 60th percentile in that table (PSYC 210 Teaching Team, 2026b).
Privitera (2018, 2024) distinguishes:

percentile point → the score value;
percentile rank → the percentage associated with its position in the distribution.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
16. Grouped Frequency Distributions
When there are many possible values, listing every score can become unwieldy.
A grouped frequency distribution combines scores into class intervals or bins of equal width (Privitera, 2018, 2024; Sigal, 2026).
Grouping helps us see the overall structure more clearly, but it creates a trade-off:

Grouping simplifies the data, but exact individual values are no longer recoverable from the grouped table.

This is an important form of information loss.

section: 18. Lower Limits, Upper Limits, and Real Limits
text:
18. Lower Limits, Upper Limits, and Real Limits
Each class interval has a lower and upper limit.
If the interval width is 5, possible apparent intervals are:

25–29
30–34
35–39
…

For whole-number data, the apparent width of 25–29 seems to be:
\[
29-25=4.
\]
But the real limits extend half a measurement unit beyond the apparent limits:
\[
24.5 \text{ to } 29.5.
\]
The real width is therefore:
\[
29.5-24.5=5.
\]
This distinction matters when constructing continuous histograms because adjacent intervals meet at real boundaries without gaps (Sigal, 2026).

Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
20. Visualizing Frequency Distributions
The lecture emphasizes three basic graphical displays:

Bar charts
Histograms
Frequency polygons

The correct choice depends on the type of variable and on what the display is intended to communicate (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
21. Bar Charts
A bar chart is typically used for discrete or categorical data.

Key visual feature

The bars do not touch.

The gaps remind us that the categories are distinct rather than positions along a continuous measurement scale.
For nominal data, categories may often be reordered without changing their meaning.
For ordinal data, the order should usually be preserved because the rank itself is meaningful.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
22. Histograms
A histogram is used for quantitative continuous data.

Key visual feature

Adjacent bars touch.

The touching bars communicate that values lie along a continuum.
Privitera (2018, 2024) gives three core rules:

bar height represents the frequency in each interval;
bar bases correspond to interval boundaries;
adjacent bars touch because the variable is continuous.

Histograms are therefore fundamentally different from bar charts, even though both use rectangular bars.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
23. Frequency Polygons
A frequency polygon represents a distribution using points connected by lines rather than bars.
It conveys the same basic information as a histogram but can make the overall shape of a distribution particularly easy to see.
Frequency polygons are appropriate for continuous quantitative data (Privitera, 2018; Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
24. What Grouping Changes
The lecture explicitly contrasts grouped and ungrouped displays:

Ungrouped distributions retain all distinct observed values.
Grouped distributions summarize observations into intervals.
Once grouped, the exact original observations are no longer recoverable from the display (Sigal, 2026).

This is not an error. It is the cost of summarization.
The analyst therefore has to decide how much detail to preserve.

section: 26. Central Tendency: A Second Way to Summarize Data
text:
26. Central Tendency: A Second Way to Summarize Data
The assigned Chapter 3 readings extend the logic of summarization.
A frequency distribution summarizes how scores are distributed.
A measure of central tendency reduces the distribution to a single value near its center (Privitera, 2018, 2024).
The three main measures are:

mean;
median;
mode.

These measures are not interchangeable. Each answers a slightly different question.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
27. The Mean
The arithmetic mean is:
\[
M=\frac{\sum X}{n}
\]
for a sample, or
\[
\mu=\frac{\sum X}{N}
\]
for a population.
The calculation is the same; the notation changes because one value describes a sample and the other a population (Privitera, 2018, 2024).
The mean is often described as the balance point of a distribution.

Important characteristic
Because every observation contributes to the mean, unusual or extreme scores can shift it substantially.
The mean is typically most informative for approximately symmetrical distributions of interval- or ratio-scale data (Privitera, 2018, 2024).

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
28. The Median
The median is the middle score after scores are ordered.
Its position is:
\[
\frac{n+1}{2}.
\]
For an odd number of observations, the median is the single middle score.
For an even number of observations, average the two middle scores.
The median is resistant to extreme values. Privitera (2018, 2024) therefore recommends it particularly for:

skewed distributions;
ordinal data;
distributions containing important outliers.

The median also corresponds to the 50th percentile.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization

text:
30. Choosing Mean, Median, or Mode
The readings summarize the choice as follows (Privitera, 2018, 2024):







Measure
Often appropriate when…




Mean
Data are interval/ratio and reasonably symmetrical


Median
Data are ordinal or skewed; outliers matter


Mode
Data are nominal or the most frequent category/value is substantively important



These are guiding principles rather than mechanical rules. The appropriate summary depends on the research question, measurement scale, and shape of the distribution.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
31. How the Concepts Fit Together
Week 2 can be understood as one sequence:
What kind of variable do I have?
↓
What does the measurement scale allow me to say?
↓
Should I preserve individual scores or group them?
↓
What frequency summaries are useful?
↓
What graph is appropriate?
↓
Would a measure of central tendency add useful information?
↓
Does the display accurately communicate the evidence?
The scale of measurement affects what mathematical summaries are meaningful. The frequency distribution shows the structure of the data. Graphs make that structure visible. Measures of central tendency compress it further into representative values.

text:
32. Important Terms







Term
Plain-language explanation




Nominal scale
Categories identified by names or labels, without meaningful order.


Ordinal scale
Ordered categories without known equal distances between categories.


Interval scale
Ordered numeric scale with equal intervals but no true zero.


Ratio scale
Interval-like scale with a meaningful zero, permitting ratio comparisons.


Discrete variable
Variable consisting of separate values or categories.


Continuous variable
Variable measured along a continuum.


Qualitative variable
Variable that differs by category or class.


Quantitative variable
Variable that differs by amount.


Frequency
Number of times a value/category occurs.


Relative frequency
Frequency divided by total (n).


Percentage
Relative frequency multiplied by 100.


Cumulative frequency
Running total of frequencies.


Cumulative percentage
Running total of percentages.


Percentile rank
Percentage of observations at or below a specified position under the course convention.


Ungrouped distribution
Frequency table listing distinct scores/categories individually.


Grouped distribution
Frequency table combining scores into class intervals.


Bin/class interval
Range of values grouped together.


Lower/upper limit
Lowest/highest apparent value assigned to an interval.


Real limits
Boundaries that extend halfway to adjacent measurable values.


Bar chart
Graph for discrete/categorical data using separated bars.


Histogram
Graph for continuous quantitative data using touching bars.


Frequency polygon
Line-based graph connecting frequencies across quantitative intervals.


Mean
Sum of scores divided by number of scores.


Median
Middle ordered score.


Mode
Most frequently occurring value/category.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
33. Common Misunderstandings

“If categories are coded with numbers, they become quantitative.”
No. The meaning of the numbers depends on the measurement process. Nominal codes remain labels.


“Ordinal numbers tell me how far apart categories are.”
No. Ordinal data provide order, not equal distance.


“Zero always means none.”
No. A true zero is a property of ratio scales. (0^C) is not an absence of temperature.


“Grouped frequency distributions are more accurate.”
They are often clearer, but they are less precise because individual values are hidden within intervals.


“All frequency tables should omit zero-frequency values.”
Not necessarily. Including missing internal values can make the scale and cumulative pattern clearer.


“Bar charts and histograms are the same thing.”
No. The gaps between bars in a bar chart communicate discrete categories; touching histogram bars represent continuity.


“A graph cannot mislead if all the numbers are correct.”
False. Axis limits, scales, binning, and graphical emphasis can substantially change the viewer’s impression.


“The mean is always the best description of the center.”
No. Outliers and skew can make the median more representative; nominal data often require the mode.


“Likert-like scales are obviously interval.”
The Week 2 sources do not agree on this. The lecture is strongly critical of that assumption, while Privitera (2024) explains why many behavioral researchers pragmatically treat rating scales as interval. Know the course convention and the methodological issue.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
34. Tutorial Preparation
A TA should be ready to move repeatedly between conceptual interpretation and calculation.

Questions students may ask

“Why is grade ordinal but height ratio?”
Grade categories have order but unequal or undefined distances between adjacent grades. Height has equal units and a meaningful zero.


“Why include a score with zero frequency?”
Because a frequency table often represents the structure of a scale, not merely the values observed. Omitting internal values can obscure gaps.


“How do I know whether to group data?”
Grouping becomes useful when many distinct values make an ungrouped table hard to read. But grouping sacrifices exact detail.


“Why do histogram bars touch?”
Because the variable is treated as continuous, and adjacent intervals meet at their real boundaries.


“How do I know which direction to calculate cumulative frequency?”
It depends on the question. Bottom-up cumulative summaries naturally answer “at or below” questions; top-down summaries answer “at or above” questions (Privitera, 2018, 2024).


“Which measure of central tendency should I use?”
Ask about both the measurement scale and the distribution:

nominal → mode;
ordinal or strongly skewed → median is often useful;
interval/ratio and roughly symmetrical → mean is often useful.

39. Week 2 Takeaway
Week 2 is fundamentally about matching the summary to the data.
Before calculating anything, ask:

What kind of variable is this, and what do its values actually mean?

Then ask:

What representation—table, grouped distribution, graph, mean, median, or mode—preserves the information I need without implying more than the data support?

That habit is more important than memorizing any single formula.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization

The Big Picture
Week 2 asks two linked questions:

What kind of variable do I have?
How should I summarize and display it?

The measurement scale determines what the values mean, and that helps determine which summaries and graphs are appropriate.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
Variable Types and NOIR

Categorical vs. continuous
Categorical variables represent qualitative categories or ordered categories.
Continuous variables represent measured quantities using a defined unit.


Nominal
Nominal values distinguish categories only.
Examples:

psychiatric diagnosis;
dominant hand;
eye colour.

There is no meaningful rank order.


Ordinal
Ordinal values have a meaningful order, but the distance between adjacent categories is not guaranteed to be equal.
Examples:

Mild, Moderate, Severe;
class rank;
letter grades.



Interval
Interval variables have equal measurement units but an arbitrary zero point.
Examples in the guide include Celsius temperature, standardized IQ scores, and calendar years.


Ratio
Ratio variables have equal units and a meaningful zero indicating absence of the measured quantity.
Examples include:

reaction time;
distance;
mass;
counts.

A useful exam reminder is that the same phenomenon can be measured on different scales depending on how it is operationalized.

section: What this question is asking you to do
text:
What this question is asking you to do
This question tests whether you can read summation notation correctly and apply the operations in the correct order. The main challenge is not arithmetic; it is deciding what is done first.
Several expressions look very similar but mean different things. For example:

\([\sum(x_i)]^2\) means sum first, then square the total.
\(\sum(x_i)^2\) means square each \(x_i\) value first, then sum.
\(\sum(x_i-y_i)\) means subtract within each paired row, then sum.
\((\sum x_i)(\sum y_i)\) means find two separate sums, then multiply them.

title: Assignment 1 — Guide and Preparation
text:
How to approach it

Write the two vectors in parallel so that each \(x_i\) stays paired with the corresponding \(y_i\).
For each subquestion, translate the notation into words before calculating.
Use BEDMAS/PEDMAS:

brackets/parentheses;
exponents;
multiplication/division;
addition/subtraction.

For a and b, simply add the values in the requested vector.
For c and d, calculate the sum first and square only after the summation is complete.
For e, calculate each paired difference \(x_i-y_i\), then add the differences.
For f, calculate each paired product \(x_iy_i\), then add the products.
For g and h, square each individual value first, then sum the squared values.
For i, calculate the paired differences, sum those differences, then square the final sum.
For j, calculate \(\sum x_i\) and \(\sum y_i\) separately, then multiply the two totals.
For k, add 3 to each \(x_i\), square each transformed value, then sum.
For l, pay close attention to the denominator: evaluate \(2^2\) according to order of operations, apply the division to each \(y_i\), and then sum.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Week 1 introduces the logic of data analysis in psychology. The central idea is that statistics is not simply a collection of formulas. It is a way to connect questions, theories, measurements, data, and evidence-based conclusions.
The lecture begins with the goals of science and then moves through the basic research process: identify something that needs explaining, decide how to measure it, formulate a research hypothesis, collect data, and analyze those data descriptively or inferentially. It also introduces the distinction between populations and samples, basic research designs, and several mathematical tools—especially summation notation—that will be used throughout the course.
The tutorials and practice materials reinforce these ideas through hands-on work with summation notation and the basic organization of data into frequency tables and histograms.

4. Variables
A variable is something that can take more than one value across people, objects, times, or conditions.
In a statistical analysis, variables can play different roles.







Variable role
Meaning




Independent variable (IV)
A variable that is manipulated or used as a predictor.


Dependent variable (DV)
A variable that is measured as the outcome or response.


Extraneous/confounding variable
Another variable that may influence the outcome and complicate interpretation.




Example: Pet therapy
The lecture uses the question of whether interaction with a dog might calm the autonomic nervous system of children with ADHD.
Possible variables include:

type of interaction: interaction with an adult vs. interaction with a dog;
blood pressure;
heart rate.

The general analytical question is whether the measured outcome differs depending on the condition.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
5. Research Hypotheses and Statistical Hypotheses
A research hypothesis is a plain-language statement about what a researcher expects to observe.
Examples from the lecture include:

Extroversion is related to school achievement.
Using mnemonics to study will affect exam performance.
Watching television while performing a task will affect reaction time.
Interacting with a dog will have a calming effect on the autonomic nervous system of children with ADHD.

These statements concern substantive psychological expectations.
A statistical hypothesis translates an expectation into a mathematical statement about population parameters.
This distinction matters because a statistical comparison only makes sense if it matches the research question and the way the variables were actually measured.

Important caution
A statistically correct calculation can still answer the wrong research question if the variables, measures, or comparison do not match the original hypothesis.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
6. Descriptive and Inferential Statistics

Descriptive statistics
Descriptive statistics summarize and organize data.
They answer questions such as:

What values occurred?
How frequently did they occur?
What is a typical score?
How spread out are the scores?
What does the distribution look like?

Descriptive statistics can be presented as numbers, tables, graphs, percentages, frequencies, and averages.


Inferential statistics
Inferential statistics use data from a sample to make a reasoned statement about a larger population.
The logic is:
Population → Sample → Data → Statistical analysis → Inference about the population
This is a conceptual leap because researchers usually observe only the sample, while their scientific question concerns the larger population.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
7. Populations, Samples, Parameters, and Statistics
These four terms belong together.







Term
Meaning




Population
The complete set of people, objects, or events of interest.


Sample
A subset of the population that is actually observed.


Parameter
A value that describes a population.


Statistic
A value that describes a sample.



For example, suppose the population is all students enrolled in an introductory statistics course. A researcher might study 80 students.

The population is all relevant students.
The sample is the 80 students studied.
The true population mean anxiety score is a parameter.
The mean anxiety score calculated from the 80 students is a statistic.

Inferential statistics use sample statistics to learn about unknown population parameters.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
8. Representativeness and Sampling Error
A sample does not automatically represent its population.
Two questions should always be asked:

Is the sample representative of the population we care about?
Could chance have produced an unusual sample?

This second issue is closely related to sampling error.
Sampling error refers to the fact that different samples drawn from the same population will not be identical. Even if a sampling procedure is reasonable, a particular sample may differ from the population simply because of chance.
This is one of the central reasons inferential statistics is necessary.

TA teaching point
Students often assume that “random sample” means “perfectly representative sample.” It does not. Random sampling reduces systematic bias, but random variation still exists.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
9. Three Basic Research Designs

Experimental design
A true experiment is designed to support a cause-and-effect conclusion.
The lecture emphasizes three important features:

Manipulation — the researcher creates different conditions.
Randomization — participants are randomly allocated to conditions.
Comparison/control — outcomes are compared across conditions.


Example
To study whether watching television affects reaction time:

participants could be randomly assigned to a TV condition or a no-TV condition;
the researcher manipulates whether television is present;
reaction time is measured in both groups.

Random assignment is important because it helps distribute other participant characteristics across conditions.



Quasi-experimental design
A quasi-experiment resembles an experiment but lacks one or more elements needed for a true experiment.
This often happens because:

the independent variable cannot be manipulated;
participants cannot be randomly assigned;
a comparison/control group is missing.

Many psychological variables are preexisting and cannot ethically or practically be randomized.


Correlational or observational design
In a correlational design, researchers measure two or more variables without manipulating them.
The purpose is to determine whether variables are related.
For example:

computer use and exercise;
extroversion and school achievement;
income and life satisfaction.

A correlational design can demonstrate a relationship, but it cannot by itself establish causation.

10. Statistical Results Need Context
The lecture makes an important cautionary point: statistics can be numerically accurate and still create a misleading impression.
Graphs are especially sensitive to choices such as:

where the vertical axis begins;
the range of values displayed;
the time period selected;
the scale of an axis;
which observations are included or excluded.

Two graphs based on the same underlying phenomenon can create very different visual impressions.

Questions to ask when reading a graph

What are the axes?
Where does each axis begin?
What range is shown?
Is the scale consistent?
What time period or cases were selected?
Does the visual size of a difference match its numerical size?

The broader lesson is that statistics should be interpreted, not merely accepted.

11. Fundamental Mathematics
The course does not require advanced mathematics, but it assumes comfort with several basic mathematical tools.

Order of operations
Use PEDMAS/BEDMAS:

Parentheses / Brackets
Exponents
Division / Multiplication
Addition / Subtraction

Changing the order can produce completely different results.


Brackets and absolute value
Parentheses and square brackets group operations.
Absolute-value brackets indicate distance from zero:
\[
|4| = 4
\]
\[
|-39| = 39
\]


Inequalities
Know the meaning of \(>\), \(<\), and \(\leq\).


Fractions
You should be able to add and subtract fractions, find common denominators, and convert fractions to decimals.


Negative numbers
\[
(-a)(b) = -ab
\]
\[
(-a)(-b) = ab
\]


Basic equations
For example:
\[
15x + 10 = 40
\]
Subtract 10 from both sides:
\[
15x = 30
\]
Then divide by 15:
\[
x = 2
\]


Exponents and square roots
\[
3^2 = 9
\]
\[
\sqrt{9} = 3
\]
\[
3^4 = 81
\]

12. Summation Notation
The Greek letter sigma, \(\Sigma\), means sum or add together.
If
\[
X = \{1,5,10\}
\]
then
\[
\sum X = 1 + 5 + 10 = 16
\]
More complete notation looks like:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i
\]
This means: add the values of \(X_i\), beginning with the first indexed value and ending with the \(n\)th value.

Indices matter
If
\[
X = \{4,8,6,3,5,6,4,2\}
\]
then
\[
\sum_{i=2}^{5} X_i = 8 + 6 + 3 + 5 = 22
\]
Only values with indices 2 through 5 are included.


Summing products
If two variables are paired,
\[
\sum XY
\]
means multiply \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) within each row and then add the resulting products.
It does not mean
\[
(\sum X)(\sum Y)
\]
unless that is explicitly written.


Squaring a sum is not the same as summing squares
These expressions are different:
\[
\left(\sum X\right)^2
\]
and
\[
\sum X^2
\]
For example, if \(X=\{1,2,3\}\):
\[
\left(\sum X\right)^2 = (1+2+3)^2 = 36
\]
but
\[
\sum X^2 = 1^2+2^2+3^2 = 14
\]
This distinction becomes extremely important later in formulas for variance and other statistics.


Parentheses prevent ambiguity
Compare:
\[
\sum(X_i + 2)
\]
with
\[
\left(\sum X_i\right)+2
\]
They are not equivalent.

A frequency table organizes a set of scores by showing how often each score—or each range of scores—occurs.

19. Important Terms







Term
Plain-language explanation




Statistics
Methods for collecting, summarizing, analyzing, interpreting, and presenting numerical observations.


Data
A set of observations or measurements.


Variable
A characteristic that can take more than one value.


Operational definition
A precise statement of how a variable is measured or observed.


Research hypothesis
A substantive expectation about what a study may find.


Statistical hypothesis
A mathematical statement about population parameters.


Descriptive statistics
Methods for organizing and summarizing observed data.


Inferential statistics
Methods for using sample data to reason about a population.


Population
The complete set of cases of interest.


Sample
A subset of the population that is observed.


Parameter
A numerical characteristic of a population.


Statistic
A numerical characteristic of a sample.


Sampling error
Difference between a sample and population that can occur because of chance sampling variation.


Independent variable
A manipulated or predictor variable.


Dependent variable
A measured outcome or response variable.


Confounding variable
Another variable that may influence the outcome and complicate interpretation.


Experiment
A design using manipulation, randomization, and comparison/control.


Quasi-experiment
An experiment-like design missing some element of experimental control.


Correlational design
A design measuring relationships among variables without manipulation.


Summation notation
Mathematical notation using \(\Sigma\) to represent addition across indexed observations.


Frequency
Number of observations having a value or falling within a class.


Relative frequency
Frequency divided by the total number of observations.


Cumulative frequency
Running total of frequencies.


Histogram
Graph showing the frequency distribution of quantitative scores.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
20. Common Misunderstandings

“Statistics proves that something is true.”
No. Statistical analysis helps quantify evidence and uncertainty. Conclusions remain dependent on the study design, measurement quality, sample, assumptions, and context.


“A sample is basically the same thing as a population.”
No. A sample is only a subset. Inferential statistics is needed precisely because we usually do not observe the whole population.


“A statistic and a parameter are interchangeable.”
No. Statistic → sample; parameter → population.


“Random assignment and random sampling are the same.”
No. Random sampling concerns how people are selected from a population. Random assignment concerns how selected participants are placed into experimental conditions.


“Correlation shows that one variable causes the other.”
No. Correlation shows a relationship, not cause.


“\(\sum X^2\) and \((\sum X)^2\) mean the same thing.”
No. One squares each score before summing; the other sums first and then squares.


“The number after sigma is always added once.”
Not necessarily. If a constant is inside the summation, it is applied once for each indexed observation.


“A histogram is an objective picture of the data.”
The data are objective observations, but the display still depends on choices such as bin width, axis range, and grouping.

25. Week 1 Takeaway
The most important lesson this week is not a formula.
It is a way of thinking:

Start with a question, define what you mean, decide how to observe it, collect evidence, summarize what you observed, and be cautious when using a sample to say something about a larger population.

The mathematical notation and frequency-table skills introduced this week are tools that support that broader reasoning process.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
The Big Picture
Week 1 is about learning the language of statistical reasoning before doing substantial statistics.
A useful chain is:
scientific question → theory → variables and hypotheses → research design → sample data → description → inference about a population
For the midterm, you should be able to recognize where each idea belongs in that chain and explain why the distinction matters.

Science, theories, variables, and hypotheses
A scientific theory is used to organize and explain observations and to generate testable expectations. Variables are the things that can differ across people, conditions, or observations. A hypothesis states an expected relationship, difference, or effect involving those variables.
For review purposes, keep the levels separate:

Theory: broader explanation.
Variable: something that can take different values.
Hypothesis: a specific expectation that can be evaluated with evidence.



Research designs
Know the basic distinction among:

Experimental designs
Quasi-experimental designs
Correlational designs

The key exam question is usually not “What is the label?” but “What kind of conclusion can this design support?”
A true experiment is the design that most directly supports a cause-and-effect conclusion because the researcher manipulates an independent variable and uses random assignment to conditions. A quasi-experiment lacks full experimental control, often because random assignment is not possible. A correlational design measures variables as they naturally occur and can establish association, but not causation.


Descriptive vs. inferential statistics
Descriptive statistics summarize the data that were actually observed.
Inferential statistics use sample information to draw conclusions about a larger population.
A reliable exam check is:

If the statement stays inside the observed sample, it is descriptive.
If it generalizes beyond the sample to a population, it is inferential.



Population vs. sample
A population is the full group the researcher wants to understand.
A sample is the subset actually observed.
The logic of the course depends on this distinction because researchers usually collect sample data but want to learn about a population.

section: 1. Why Do We Need Measures of Center?
text:
1. Why Do We Need Measures of Center?
A frequency distribution tells us how scores are distributed, but researchers often also want a single value that summarizes what is typical or representative.
The Week 3 lecture frames central tendency as an attempt to locate the “center” of a sample or population, while emphasizing that “center” can mean different things (Sigal, 2026).
The three standard measures are:

Mode
Median
Mean

Each defines “center” differently.



Measure
Basic idea




Mode
Most frequently occurring value/category


Median
Middle position in terms of frequency


Mean
Arithmetic balance point in terms of magnitudes



The fact that there are three measures is not redundancy. They behave differently and are useful under different conditions.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
2. The Mode
The mode is the value or category that occurs most often.
For:
\[
X=\{0,1,2,2,3\},
\]
the mode is:
\[
2.
\]
The lecture recommends a simple procedure:

inspect the values;
sort if useful;
count frequencies;
identify the value with the highest frequency (Sigal, 2026).


More than one mode
For:
\[
X=\{0,1,1,1,1,2,2,3,3,3,3,5\},
\]
both 1 and 3 occur four times.
The distribution is therefore bimodal.
A distribution may be:

unimodal — one mode;
bimodal — two modes;
multimodal — more than two modes;
nonmodal — no value occurs more often than the others.



Why the mode is special
The mode can be used with categorical data because it depends only on frequency.
For example, if browser preference is categorical, the “most common browser” is meaningful even though an arithmetic mean of browser codes would not be.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
3. The Median
The median is the value that divides an ordered distribution in half based on frequency.
It is also the 50th percentile (Sigal, 2026).
The median is not necessarily an observed score.

Basic position rule
A common quick rule for the median position is:
\[
\frac{n+1}{2}.
\]
For an odd sample size:
\[
X=\{11,5,8,10,3\}.
\]
Sort the values:
\[
\{3,5,8,10,11\}.
\]
Because:
\[
\frac{5+1}{2}=3,
\]
the median is the third score:
\[
Md=8.
\]

4. Median With an Even Number of Scores
Suppose:
\[
X=\{3,3,4,5,7,8\}.
\]
Then:
\[
\frac{6+1}{2}=3.5.
\]
The median falls halfway between positions 3 and 4.
Average those two scores:
\[
Md=\frac{4+5}{2}=4.5.
\]
For ordinary ungrouped data, this is the familiar textbook procedure.
However, the Week 3 lecture introduces a more general interpolation method because the instructor wants students to think about the median as a location within an interval, especially when ties or grouped data are involved (Sigal, 2026).
