7. A Course-Specific Median Convention
There is an important methodological point here.
For simple ungrouped raw data, many statistics texts define the median as the middle observed score, or the average of the two middle observed scores when (n) is even. The Week 3 lecture deliberately goes beyond that quick rule and uses interpolation based on cumulative frequency—even when scores are tied—because the instructor wants students to conceptualize percentiles as positions within score intervals (Sigal, 2026).
The supplemental median handout makes this intention explicit. It states that the quick ((n+1)/2) rule can be misleading for binned data with many ties and demonstrates a grouped age example in which the median is estimated as 24.1 rather than simply reporting the category 24–26 (PSYC 210 Teaching Team, 2026a).

For this course
When solving course problems that ask for the formula-based median:

Use the interpolation procedure demonstrated in the lecture and supplemental handout.

Do not silently substitute the simpler textbook convention when the problem is clearly designed around cumulative frequency and real limits.

11. The Mean
The mean is the arithmetic average.
For a sample:
\[
\bar{x}
=
\frac{\sum x_i}{n}.
\]
The lecture notes that APA-style reporting commonly uses (M) for a sample mean, while () is used for a population mean (Sigal, 2026).
For:
\[
X=\{3,7,4,6\},
\]
\[
\bar{x}
=
\frac{3+7+4+6}{4}
=
\frac{20}{4}
=
5.
\]
Conceptually, the mean is a balance point based on magnitudes.

text:
12. Sample and Population Mean Notation
The lecture distinguishes:

sample mean: ({x}) or (M);
population mean: ().

The calculation itself is structurally the same:
\[
M=\frac{\sum X}{n},
\]
and:
\[
\mu=\frac{\sum X}{N}.
\]
The symbols remind us whether the calculation describes a sample or the entire population of interest.

text:
13. The Weighted Mean
A simple average of group means is only correct when the groups contribute equal weight.
Suppose:

Group 1: ({x}_1=6, n_1=20)
Group 2: ({x}_2=15, n_2=3)

It would be wrong to calculate:
\[
\frac{6+15}{2}=10.5.
\]
The groups are not equally large.
Instead:
\[
\bar{x}_C
=

{n_1+n_2}.
\]
Because:
\[
\sum X_1=120
\]

\[
\sum X_2=45,
\]
the combined mean is:
\[
\bar{x}_C
=
\frac{120+45}{20+3}
=
\frac{165}{23}
=
7.17.
\]
The larger group contributes more information and therefore more weight (Sigal, 2026).

text:
15. How the Mean Changes
The Week 3 worksheet asks students to explore how transformations affect the mean (PSYC 210 Teaching Team, 2026b).
The key patterns are:

Change one score
Changing one observation changes the mean because the total sum changes.


Add a constant to every score
If every observation increases by (c),
\[
M_{\text{new}}=M_{\text{old}}+c.
\]


Multiply every score by a constant
If every observation is multiplied by (c),
\[
M_{\text{new}}=cM_{\text{old}}.
\]


Subtract the mean from every score
If:
\[
Y_i=X_i-M,
\]
then:
\[
\bar{Y}=0.
\]
This is because deviations from the mean sum to zero.


Add a new score
A new score above the old mean pulls the mean upward.
A new score below the old mean pulls the mean downward.
A new score equal to the old mean leaves the mean unchanged.

section: 16. Why Do We Need Three Measures of Center?
text:
16. Why Do We Need Three Measures of Center?
The lecture answers this by asking what kinds of data and distributions we have (Sigal, 2026).

Mode
Useful for:

categorical/discrete data;
identifying the most common response;
describing modality.



Median
Useful when:

scores are ordinal;
the distribution has extreme scores or outliers;
a robust description of the middle is desirable.



Mean
Useful in many quantitative settings because it incorporates the magnitude of every score.
The key principle is:

The best measure depends on the structure of the data.

19. Mean, Median, Mode, and Shape
The lecture presents a useful heuristic:

Approximately symmetric / bell-shaped
\[
\text{mean} \approx \text{median} \approx \text{mode}.
\]


Positive skew
\[
\text{mean}>\text{median}>\text{mode}.
\]


Negative skew
\[
\text{mean}<\text{median}<\text{mode}.
\]
The reason is that the mean is particularly sensitive to extreme values and is pulled toward the long tail (Sigal, 2026).
These relationships are useful descriptive clues, not universal mathematical identities for every irregular dataset.

text:
22. The Range
The range is:
\[
\text{Range}
=
X_{\max}-X_{\min}.
\]
It is the simplest measure of variability.
For:
\[
1,2,3,4,5,
\]
\[
\text{Range}=5-1=4.
\]

Limitation
The range uses only two observations:

the minimum;
the maximum.

Therefore, a single extreme score can drastically inflate it.
Privitera (2018, 2024) emphasizes that the range is most informative when important outliers are absent.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
23. Interquartile Range
The interquartile range (IQR) describes the spread of the middle 50% of a distribution.
It is:
\[
IQR=Q_3-Q_1.
\]
where:

(Q_1) = 25th percentile;
(Q_2) = median / 50th percentile;
(Q_3) = 75th percentile.

Because the top and bottom 25% are excluded, the IQR is less sensitive to extreme scores than the full range (Privitera, 2018, 2024).

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
24. From Deviation to Variance
Suppose we want to quantify how far scores are from the mean.
For each score:
\[
\text{deviation}
=
X_i-M.
\]
If the data are:
\[
X=\{3,4,5,6,12\},
\]
the mean is:
\[
M=6.
\]
The deviations are:
\[
-3,-2,-1,0,6.
\]
But:
\[
\sum(X_i-M)=0.
\]
Positive and negative deviations cancel.
Therefore, simply averaging raw signed deviations would always make variability look like zero.
This is why deviations are squared before they are summed.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
25. Sum of Squares
The sum of squares (SS) is:
\[
SS
=
\sum(X_i-M)^2
\]
for a sample, or:
\[
SS
=
\sum(X_i-\mu)^2
\]
for a population.
Because each deviation is squared:

negative signs disappear;
larger deviations contribute more;
(SS).

If every observation is identical, every deviation is zero, and:
\[
SS=0.
\]
Privitera (2018, 2024) describes SS as the sum of squared deviations from the mean and the numerator used in the variance formulas.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
26. Population Variance
Population variance is:
\[
\sigma^2
=
\frac{
\sum(X_i-\mu)^2
}{N}
=
\frac{SS}{N}.
\]
The lecture example uses:
\[
X=\{1,0,6,1\}
\]
with:
\[
\mu=2.
\]
The deviations are:
\[
-1,-2,4,-1.
\]
Squared deviations:
\[
1,4,16,1.
\]
Thus:
\[
SS=22.
\]
Population variance is:
\[
\sigma^2
=
\frac{22}{4}
=
5.5.
\]

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
27. Standard Deviation for a Population
The population standard deviation is the square root of the population variance:
\[
\sigma
=
\sqrt{\sigma^2}.
\]
For the previous example:
\[
\sigma
=
\sqrt{5.5}
\approx
2.35.
\]
Variance is expressed in squared units.
Standard deviation returns the measure of spread to the original units of measurement (Privitera, 2018, 2024; Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
28. Sample Variance
When the observed data are a sample rather than the entire population, the Week 3 materials use:
\[
s^2
=
\frac{
\sum(X_i-\bar{X})^2
}{n-1}
=
\frac{SS}{n-1}.
\]
Using the same values:
\[
X=\{1,0,6,1\},
\]
we still have:
\[
SS=22.
\]
But now:
\[
s^2
=
\frac{22}{4-1}
=
\frac{22}{3}
\approx
7.33.
\]
The sample standard deviation is:
\[
s
=
\sqrt{7.33}
\approx
2.71.
\]

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
29. Why Does Sample Variance Use (n-1)?
This is one of the most important conceptual ideas in Week 3.
If we calculate sample variance using (n), it tends to underestimate the population variance.
Dividing by:
\[
n-1
\]
makes the sample variance a better estimator of population variance on average (Privitera, 2018, 2024; Sigal, 2026).
Privitera describes this as an unbiased estimator:

Across repeated random samples, variance calculated with (n-1) equals the population variance on average.

This correction is often associated with Bessel’s correction.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
30. Degrees of Freedom
The denominator:
\[
n-1
\]
is also the degrees of freedom for sample variance.
Degrees of freedom can be understood as the number of scores that remain free to vary once the sample mean is known.
Suppose a sample contains three scores and has:
\[
M=4.
\]
If two scores are:
\[
3,\ 4,
\]
then the third cannot be arbitrary.
Because the three scores must sum to:
\[
3(4)=12,
\]
the missing value must be:
\[
5.
\]
Thus only:
\[
n-1
\]
scores are independently free to vary (Privitera, 2018, 2024; Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
31. Standard Deviation
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
For a sample:
\[
s=\sqrt{s^2}
=
\sqrt{\frac{SS}{n-1}}.
\]
For a population:
\[
\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}
=
\sqrt{\frac{SS}{N}}.
\]
The standard deviation gives a measure of the typical distance of scores from the mean in the original scale of measurement (Privitera, 2018, 2024).

Interpretation

smaller SD → scores are more tightly clustered around the mean;
larger SD → scores are more widely spread.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
32. Variance vs. Standard Deviation



Quantity
What it measures
Units




Variance
Average squared spread from the mean
Squared units


Standard deviation
Spread around the mean
Original units



For example, if heights are measured in inches:

variance is in inches squared;
standard deviation is in inches.

This is one reason standard deviation is easier to interpret directly.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
section: 33. What Happens When Scores Are Transformed?
text:
33. What Happens When Scores Are Transformed?
The Week 3 worksheet explicitly asks students to investigate transformations (PSYC 210 Teaching Team, 2026b).

Add or subtract the same constant from every score
If:
\[
Y_i=X_i+c,
\]
then the mean shifts:
\[
M_Y=M_X+c.
\]
But distances from the mean do not change.
Therefore:
\[
s_Y=s_X
\]
and:
\[
s_Y^2=s_X^2.
\]


Multiply every score by a constant
If:
\[
Y_i=cX_i,
\]
then:
\[
M_Y=cM_X,
\]
\[
s_Y=|c|s_X,
\]
and:
\[
s_Y^2=c^2s_X^2.
\]
These relationships are central to understanding standardization later in the course.

That is the larger Week 3 goal:

A useful description of a dataset normally requires more than one statistic.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
36. What Should Be Reported Together?
Measures of center and variability are most informative when interpreted together.
For many quantitative variables, researchers commonly report:
\[
M\pm SD.
\]
The mean tells us about the center.
The standard deviation tells us about spread around that center.
Privitera (2018, 2024) emphasizes that the standard deviation is especially informative when reported with the mean.
For skewed distributions or variables with important outliers, a median paired with a robust measure such as the IQR may be more informative.

What is the distribution’s center?

Term
Plain-language explanation




Mode
Most frequently occurring value or category.


Median
Middle position of an ordered distribution; 50th percentile.


Mean
Arithmetic average; balance point based on magnitudes.


Weighted mean
Mean in which groups/values contribute according to their weights or sample sizes.


Skewness
Asymmetry of a distribution.


Positive skew
Long tail toward larger values.


Negative skew
Long tail toward smaller values.


Variability
Degree to which scores are dispersed or spread.


Range
Maximum minus minimum.


Quartile
Boundary dividing a distribution into four parts.

(Q_3-Q_1); spread of the middle 50%.


Deviation
Difference between a score and the mean.

(SS/N).

(SS/(n-1)).

Square root of variance; spread in original units.

text:
40. Common Misunderstandings

“The mode has to be a number.”
No. The mode can be a category.


“A distribution can only have one mode.”
No. It can be bimodal or multimodal.


“The median is always an observed score.”
No. It can lie between observed scores or be interpolated within an interval.


“The mean is always the best measure of center.”
No. Extreme scores can make it misleading.


“A positively skewed distribution has most scores on the right.”
No. The tail points right; most observations are concentrated more toward the lower side.


“Variance and standard deviation are the same thing.”
No. Standard deviation is the square root of variance.


“Standard deviation can be negative.”
No. Variability cannot be negative.


“Sample and population variance use the same denominator.”
No. Population variance divides by (N); sample variance divides by (n-1).


“Using (n-1) is just a strange convention.”
No. It corrects the systematic downward bias that occurs when sample variance is calculated with (n), and it corresponds to the degrees of freedom available after estimating the mean.


“If I add 10 to every score, standard deviation increases by 10.”
No. The mean shifts, but the distances between scores and their mean remain unchanged.


“If I multiply every score by 10, variance also multiplies by 10.”
No. Standard deviation multiplies by 10; variance multiplies by:
\[
10^2=100.
\]

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
41. Tutorial Preparation
A TA should be ready to explain both procedures and why the procedures work.

“Why are there three measures of central tendency?”
Because they define “center” differently and respond differently to scale, skewness, and outliers.


“Why can’t I average group means?”
You can only do that directly when the groups contribute equally. With unequal sample sizes, use a weighted mean.


“Why does the mean move toward an outlier?”
Because every score contributes its magnitude to the total sum.


“Why does the median resist outliers?”
Because it depends primarily on ordered position rather than the magnitude of extreme values.


“Why do we square deviations?”
Because signed deviations sum to zero. Squaring prevents cancellation and produces a positive measure of spread.


“Why take the square root afterward?”
Because variance is in squared units. The square root produces standard deviation in the original units.


“Why (n-1)?”
Because estimating the sample mean consumes one degree of freedom, and dividing by (n-1) corrects the average downward bias in sample variance.


“Why does adding a constant not change SD?”
Because every score and the mean shift by exactly the same amount, so the deviations remain unchanged.

Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
Week 5 is the major transition from descriptive statistics to the foundations of inferential statistics.
In Week 4, the course used z scores and the normal distribution to ask:

How unusual is an individual score relative to a population distribution?

Week 5 extends exactly the same logic to a new question:

How unusual is a sample mean relative to the population it came from?

The lecture begins with basic probability and then returns to the research process. Researchers usually want to make statements about populations, but they almost never observe whole populations. Instead, they collect samples and use sample statistics to estimate population parameters. Because different random samples produce different results, this introduces sampling error (Sigal, 2026).
The key conceptual sequence is:
Probability
↓
Samples vary
↓
Sampling error
↓
Sampling distributions
↓
Central Limit Theorem
↓
Standard error
↓
z for sample means
↓
Probability of obtaining a sample mean
This is the theoretical bridge to hypothesis testing in Week 6.

text:
3. Independent and Dependent Events
The lecture distinguishes two situations.

Independent events
One event does not change the probability of another.
Example:

Draw a card, replace it, and draw again.

Because the first draw is replaced, the second draw begins from the same deck composition.


Dependent events
One event changes the probability of another.
Example:

Draw two cards without replacement.

After the first card is removed, the second draw comes from a changed sample space (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
4. The “And” Rule
For independent events, the lecture uses:
\[
P(A\cap B)
=
P(A)\times P(B).
\]
For example, rolling two fair dice and obtaining a particular result on each die requires multiplying the relevant probabilities.

Important scope condition
The simple multiplication rule above applies when the events are independent.
For dependent events, the second probability must reflect the changed condition:
\[
P(A\cap B)
=
P(A)P(B\mid A).
\]
This distinction is consistent with the lecture’s preceding contrast between independent and dependent events.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
5. The “Or” Rule
For mutually exclusive outcomes, the lecture uses:
\[
P(A\cup B)
=
P(A)+P(B).
\]
Example:

On one die roll, what is the probability of rolling a 6 or a 1?

Because a single roll cannot be both 6 and 1:
\[
P(6\text{ or }1)
=
\frac16+\frac16
=
\frac26
=
\frac13.
\]

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem

text:
8. The Gambler’s Fallacy
The lecture immediately warns against misinterpreting long-run regularity.
The gambler’s fallacy is the belief that an outcome becomes more or less likely merely because of a recent sequence of similar outcomes.
For independent trials, previous outcomes do not change the probability of the next outcome.
If a fair coin has produced five heads in a row:
\[
P(H\text{ on next flip})=0.50.
\]
The law of large numbers concerns long-run aggregate behavior, not a force that makes the next trial “correct” a recent streak.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
9. Rare Events Still Occur
The lecture uses an XKCD example to make a related point: an event with a very small probability can still occur.
A rare event is not an impossible event.
This distinction becomes important later when inferential statistics asks how surprising an observed result is under a model.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
10. Week 4 vs. Week 5
Week 4 asked about the probability of an individual score.
If population mean and standard deviation are known:
\[
z
=
\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}.
\]
Week 5 asks:

What if the quantity we observe is not a single score, but a sample mean?

This shift from scores to statistics is the central move in Week 5 (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
11. Population, Sample, and Sampling
A population is the full group of interest.
A sample is a subset drawn from that population.
Sampling is the process by which observations are selected.
Suppose verbal IQ is defined in a population with:
\[
\mu=100
\]
and:
\[
\sigma=15.
\]
Different random samples from that population will produce different:

sample means;
sample standard deviations.

They will not generally reproduce the population parameters exactly (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
12. Parameters vs. Statistics
A parameter describes a population.
Examples:
\[
\mu,\quad \sigma.
\]
A statistic describes a sample.
Examples:
\[
\bar{x},\quad s.
\]
In the lecture simulation, the population is fixed at:
\[
\mu=100,\quad \sigma=15,
\]
yet sample means vary considerably across small samples.
This is not a contradiction.
It is the expected consequence of random sampling.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
13. Sampling Error
The lecture defines the mismatch between a sample statistic and its population parameter as sampling error (Sigal, 2026).
For example:
\[
\bar{x}-\mu
\]
can differ from zero simply because the sample contains only some members of the population.
Sampling error does not automatically imply:

a mistake;
poor measurement;
biased conduct;
bad statistics.

It can arise purely by chance.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
14. Why Larger Samples Help
The lecture states:

The larger the sample, the more representative it is, on average, of the population it was drawn from (Sigal, 2026).

This is a probabilistic statement, not a guarantee.
A larger sample can still be biased if the sampling process is systematically unrepresentative.
But under appropriate random sampling, increasing sample size reduces chance fluctuation in estimates such as the sample mean.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
15. Small Samples Fluctuate More
The lecture compares repeated samples of different sizes from a population with:
\[
\mu=100,\quad \sigma=15.
\]
Very small samples produce highly variable means.
As sample size increases, the sample means tend to cluster more closely around 100.
The lecture’s series from (n=1), (2), (10), (25), to (1000) visually demonstrates the increasing stability of the mean (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 16. One Sample Is Not a Sampling Distribution
text:
16. One Sample Is Not a Sampling Distribution
A single sample produces one sample mean.
A sampling distribution requires thinking across repeated possible samples.
This distinction is essential:

distribution of scores → individual observations;
sampling distribution of the mean → means calculated from many samples.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
17. Definition of a Sampling Distribution
The lecture defines a sampling distribution as:

the distribution of a sample statistic for all possible random samples of a particular size (n) that can be obtained from a population (Sigal, 2026).

The statistic might be:

a mean;
a variance;
another sample statistic.

Week 5 focuses primarily on the sample mean.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
19. The “Mean of Means”
If we collect many random samples and average their sample means, that average approaches the population mean.
This is why the sample mean is described as an unbiased estimator of the population mean.
Formally:
\[
\mu_{\bar X}
=
\mu.
\]
Privitera likewise states that the sample mean equals the population mean on average across random samples (Privitera, 2018, 2024).

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 20. The Three Features Used in Lecture
text:
20. The Three Features Used in Lecture
The lecture states the Central Limit Theorem in terms of the sampling distribution of sample means.
For a population with mean () and standard deviation (), the sampling distribution of means for samples of size (n) has:

Center
\[
\mu_{\bar X}
=
\mu.
\]


Width
\[
\sigma_{\bar X}
=
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]


Shape
The sampling distribution becomes approximately normal as sample size increases (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 21. Center: The Sampling Distribution Is Centered on ()
text:
21. Center: The Sampling Distribution Is Centered on ()
The first important property is:
\[
\mu_{\bar X}=\mu.
\]
This means the sample mean is unbiased.
Individual sample means can lie above or below (), but across repeated random samples they center on the true population mean.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 22. Width: Sample Means Vary Less Than Raw Scores
text:
22. Width: Sample Means Vary Less Than Raw Scores
The standard deviation of a sampling distribution of means is called the standard error.
If the population standard deviation is:
\[
\sigma,
\]
then:
\[
SE_{\bar X}
=
\sigma_{\bar X}
=
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]
Because:
\[
\sqrt{n}\ge1,
\]
the standard error cannot exceed () when (n).
Thus sample means fluctuate less than individual raw scores (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 23. Shape: Why Sampling Distributions Become More Normal
text:
23. Shape: Why Sampling Distributions Become More Normal
The lecture shows strongly positively skewed samples followed by a sampling distribution of their means that is much more nearly normal.
This is one of the most important conceptual visuals of Week 5.
The individual observations can be non-normal.
Yet the distribution of repeated sample means can become approximately normal.
This is what allows normal-probability tools to be applied to sample means even when the original population is not perfectly normal, subject to the conditions underlying the CLT (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
24. A Nuance About the CLT
The lecture emphasizes increasing sample size.
The 2024 Privitera text adds a useful qualification: normality of a sampling distribution can also be understood in terms of the number of samples or replications represented in the sampling distribution, not only the size of each sample (Privitera, 2024).
For this course, the practical focus remains:

As (n) increases, the sampling distribution of the mean becomes narrower and increasingly normal under the CLT framework.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
25. What Is Standard Error?
The lecture describes the standard error as the width of a sampling distribution (Sigal, 2026).
For the mean:
\[
SE_{\bar X}
=
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]
Privitera defines the standard error of the mean as the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of sample means (Privitera, 2018, 2024).

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
26. What Standard Error Measures
Standard error describes the typical amount by which sample means fluctuate around the population mean across repeated random sampling.
Conceptually:

Standard deviation describes variability among individual scores.


Standard error describes variability among sample statistics.

These should not be confused.

text:

28. Effect of Population Variability
Holding (n) constant:
\[
SE
=
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Therefore:

larger () → larger SE;
smaller () → smaller SE.

A more variable population produces less precise sample-mean estimates.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
29. Precision and Standard Error
The lecture interprets standard error as an indicator of how accurately a sample statistic represents a population parameter.
Smaller SE means sample means cluster more tightly around ().
Larger SE means greater sampling variability.
Thus:

Smaller standard error = greater precision of the sample mean as an estimator of the population mean.

33. Revisiting z
For an individual raw score:

36. Why Sample Size Changes the z Score
A difference of 3 points from () is not equally surprising for all sample sizes.
Larger samples have smaller standard error.
Therefore a 3-point departure represents more standard-error units when (n) is large.
This is one of the deepest conceptual points in Week 5:

The unusualness of a sample mean depends not only on how far it is from the population mean, but also on how much sampling variability we expect.

text:
37. From z to Probability
Once a sample mean has been standardized:
\[
z
=
\frac{\bar X-\mu}{SE},
\]
we can use the standard normal table exactly as in Week 4.
The new interpretation is:

We are no longer asking about the probability of an individual raw score.

We are asking:

How probable is a sample mean of this size, given a population model and sample size?

38. This Is the Bridge to Hypothesis Testing
The lecture explicitly identifies this result as the foundation for Week 6.
If we can determine how likely a sample mean is under specified population parameters, we can ask whether an observed sample is sufficiently unusual to challenge a null model.
That logic becomes formalized as hypothesis testing (Sigal, 2026).

The worksheet imagines students each observing 100 cars and counting seat-belt use.
Across the class:

\]

40. Is 62 Suspicious?
One student reports:
\[
X=62.
\]
Using the z formula:
\[
z
=
\frac{62-44}{7}
=
\frac{18}{7}
\approx
2.57.
\]
The worksheet key describes this as a very rare value given the hypothetical class distribution.
This does not prove fabrication.
It means the observation is unusual enough to warrant scrutiny under the assumed model.

section: 41. Do Not Confuse These Two Distributions
text:
41. Do Not Confuse These Two Distributions

Distribution of scores
Contains individual observations:
\[
X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n.
\]
Its standard deviation is:
\[
\sigma.
\]


Sampling distribution of the mean
Contains sample means:
\[
\bar X_1,\bar X_2,\ldots
\]
Its standard deviation is:
\[
SE_{\bar X}
=
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\]
The sampling distribution is narrower whenever:
\[
n>1.
\]

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 42. Why Means Fluctuate Less Than Scores
text:
42. Why Means Fluctuate Less Than Scores
A sample mean averages multiple observations.
Very high and very low observations tend to offset one another.
Therefore means are more stable than individual observations.
Increasing (n) strengthens this stabilizing effect.
This is why:
\[
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
<
\sigma
\]
for (n>1).

section: 45. A Nuance About the Central Limit Theorem
text:
45. A Nuance About the Central Limit Theorem
The lecture states that as sample size increases, the sampling distribution becomes approximately normal.
Privitera (2024) adds that increasing the number of repeated samples or replications can also reveal the normal form of the sampling distribution even at a fixed sample size.
This is a useful theoretical refinement.
For this course’s practical calculations, the key working relationship remains:
\[
SE=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
\]
and increasing (n) decreases sampling variability.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 46. “A larger sample always gives the correct population mean.”
text:
46. “A larger sample always gives the correct population mean.”
No.
A larger sample reduces random sampling variability, but any particular sample can still differ from the population.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 47. “Sampling error means somebody made a mistake.”
text:
47. “Sampling error means somebody made a mistake.”
No.
Sampling error is the natural difference between a sample statistic and the population parameter it estimates.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 48. “Standard deviation and standard error are the same.”
text:
48. “Standard deviation and standard error are the same.”
No.

SD describes variability among observations.
SE describes variability among sample statistics across repeated samples.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 49. “The CLT says the original population becomes normal.”
text:
49. “The CLT says the original population becomes normal.”
No.
The CLT concerns the sampling distribution of the statistic, especially the sample mean.
The original population can remain skewed.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 50. “The mean of every sample equals the population mean.”
text:
50. “The mean of every sample equals the population mean.”
No.
The sample mean equals the population mean on average across random samples.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 51. “If a sample mean is far from (), the sample must be wrong.”
text:
51. “If a sample mean is far from (), the sample must be wrong.”
No.
Rare samples can occur.
Probability measures how surprising the sample is under the assumed model; it does not by itself identify the cause.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 52. “The law of large numbers means a streak must reverse soon.”
text:
52. “The law of large numbers means a streak must reverse soon.”
No.
That is the gambler’s fallacy.
Long-run stabilization does not make independent future trials compensate for recent outcomes.

title: Week 05 — Probability, Sampling Distributions, and the Central Limit Theorem
section: 53. Questions a TA Should Be Ready to Answer
text:
53. Questions a TA Should Be Ready to Answer

“What is the difference between a sample distribution and a sampling distribution?”
A sample distribution contains individual data values from one sample.
A sampling distribution contains values of a statistic calculated from many possible samples.


“What exactly is standard error?”
The standard deviation of a sampling distribution.


“Why does SE get smaller when n gets larger?”
Because:
\[
SE=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Larger samples average out more random fluctuation.


“Why is the sampling distribution centered at ()?”
Because the sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean.


“Why can skewed data produce an approximately normal sampling distribution?”
That is the CLT: repeated sample means are more regular than the individual raw values from which they are calculated.


“Why does the same (X) have a larger z score for a bigger n?”
Because a larger sample has a smaller SE, so the same raw difference from () is more unusual in standard-error units.

text:
64. Week 5 Takeaway
Week 5 shifts the unit of reasoning from an individual score to a sample statistic.
A single score is standardized using:
\[
z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}.
\]
A sample mean is standardized using:
\[
z
=
\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}.
\]
The denominator:
\[
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
\]
is the standard error.
That one change captures the main idea of Week 5:

Sample means have their own probability distribution.

The Central Limit Theorem tells us about its:

center;
width;
shape.

Once we know those, we can ask:

How probable is the sample mean we actually observed?

That is the direct conceptual doorway to hypothesis testing.

Week 5 shifts the unit of analysis from an individual score to a sample mean.
The key reasoning chain is:
population → many possible random samples → many possible sample means → sampling distribution → probability of the sample mean we actually observed
